t: How To Handle Students Who Lie And Deny
q: But because you’re in the good habit of letting misbehavior play out , you decide to watch a bit longer before jumping in.
But doing so would draw you into an argument. It would put you on equal footing with the student. It would turn into a your-word-against-theirs battle royal.

You should only approach a student to give a consequence when you know the truth. This underscores the importance of letting misbehavior play out, of eliminating any plausible deniability, of leaving no doubt who is responsible and what rule was broken.
With the truth on your side, there is no reason for debate. There is no reason to ask why . There is no reason to allow the student to lie to you or deny their involvement.
After delivering your consequence, turn on your heel and walk away. Nothing else needs to be said, and waiting for a response is an invitation to argue.

By calmly—even matter-of-factly—delivering your consequences with truth on your side, and then walking away, you avoid the behaviors students have used since time immemorial to sidestep accountability.

When you do what you say you will, when you handle accountability fairly and consistently, when you show your students how much you care by safeguarding their right to learn and enjoy school without interference, chaos, or drama . . .

t: Are You Encouraging Your Students Too Much? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/11/15/are-you-encouraging-your-students-too-much/
q: By being judicious with your encouragement, by picking your spots and selectively choosing the right moments, your words will have greater impact.
A good rule of thumb is to never encourage students for something they’ve already proven they can do successfully—like a common routine, for example.
To accomplish something difficult of their own accord, after all, is rocket fuel for their intrinsic motivational engine . And if you’re not careful, your words can siphon the supply.
For example, the next time you send your students off for independent work, whether individually or in groups, resolve to hold back any encouragement for the first five minutes.
Often, to not encourage is the greatest encouragement. It strengthens, matures, and fills with enduring confidence.
Throttle back on using your words and voice to motivate your students and instead shift your focus to a more powerful lever.
x: Linsin argues that constant, reflexive encouragement backfires because it dilutes into background noise students eventually tune out.
His central rule of thumb is to withhold encouragement for tasks students have already proven they can do, reserving it for moments of genuine struggle or challenge.

q: What follows are seven steps that will allow you to handle this surprisingly common situation with grace and sensitivity, while all but removing the chances of it happening again.
Here at SCM we typically don’t recommend private meetings with students regarding their behavior. In this case, however, it’s warranted.
Recount the exact actions and words the student used that triggered your instinct that their behavior was disrespectful. Then simply inform them that it crossed the line.
Finish your conversation with a promise that if it happens again, you’ll enforce a consequence.
And enforcing consequences for behavior your students don’t understand to be wrong will jeopardize your relationship with them.
The good news is that body language and tone of voice will always tell you whether to enforce a consequence immediately or pull the student aside for a brief lesson.

t: When And Why You Should Leave Your Students Alone ents-alone/
q: The picture of an entire class lost in their work is the most beautiful sight in teaching.
For some this is done out of necessity. Their lessons and classroom management skills aren’t strong enough to support their students through more than a few minutes of truly independent work.
Exceptional teachers, on the other hand, know that their effectiveness is tied to how well and how long their students are able to work without their direct input.

You know you’re on the right track when no hands go up in the air, no one looks in your direction, and you have an intense desire to become invisible—for fear of disrupting the tender hum of production coursing throughout the room.
In this day and age, far too much emphasis is placed on helping individual students and not nearly enough on empowering them to take ownership of their education.

To reverse this devastating trend, work on increasing the amount of time your students spend engaged, engrossed, and immersed in learning activities devoid of your hovering presence, even if in the beginning it’s only a few minutes a day
x: Constant teacher hovering during independent work fosters learned helplessness and weak listening skills.
Build independent work stamina gradually, starting with even just a few minutes of unsupported work time per day.
Linsin contrasts teachers who constantly hover, reteach, and redirect during independent work with those who step back and let students work through challenges on their own.
